lessons.title: Greetings for Any Time of Day
lessons.objective: Greet a coworker correctly at any time of day and write a greeting question correctly.
lessons.hook: Your first words to a Peruvian coworker set the tone of the whole conversation.
lessons.aside: In Peru people usually greet everyone in the room when they arrive, even on a video call.
lessons.explain: Hola means hello. Spanish also has greetings tied to the time of day. Buenos días means good morning. Buenas tardes is used in the afternoon. Buenas noches is used in the evening and at night. Written questions start with ¿ and end with ?, as in ¿Cómo estás? ¿Cómo estás? is informal, and ¿Cómo está? is formal (usted). Example: at 3 pm a Peruvian colleague joins a call and says 'Buenas tardes, ¿cómo está?' That is a polite afternoon greeting.
key_facts: Buenos días means good morning.
Buenas tardes is used in the afternoon.
Buenas noches is used in the evening and at night.
Written questions start with ¿ and end with ?.
¿Cómo estás? is informal; ¿Cómo está? is formal (usted).
fixes: Writes 'como estas' without the opening ¿ and without accent marks.
angles: Think of a clock. Spanish greetings split the day into three blocks: morning, afternoon and night. Each block has its own greeting. Which block is 9 pm in?
A Spanish question has punctuation at both ends, like a pair of brackets around the sentence. Picture a question about where someone is from. Where would each mark go?
claims: Buenas tardes is used in the afternoon.
Buenas noches is used in the evening and at night.

items.q: It is 8 am. Which greeting fits?
items.why: Buenos días is the morning greeting.
misconceptions: Thinks buenas tardes covers the morning.
Thinks buenas noches is a general greeting.
Thinks an invented form is a standard greeting.

misconceptions: Thinks only the opening mark is needed and accents can be left off.
Thinks Spanish questions are punctuated like English ones.

lessons.title: Spanish Sounds and Spelling
lessons.objective: Pronounce Spanish vowels, silent h, ñ and stressed syllables correctly.
lessons.hook: Clear pronunciation lets coworkers understand you even when your grammar is still simple.
lessons.explain: Spanish has five vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u. Each vowel keeps the same short, clean sound in every word. The letter h is silent, so 'hola' sounds like 'o-la'. The letter ñ sounds like the 'ny' in 'canyon', so 'mañana' sounds like 'ma-nya-na'. The accent mark shows which syllable is stressed. In 'está' you stress the last syllable: es-TÁ.
key_facts: Spanish has five vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u.
The letter h is silent.
ñ sounds like the 'ny' in 'canyon'.
The accent mark shows which syllable is stressed.

predict.q: How do you think 'hora' (hour) is pronounced?

angles: English vowels change sound from word to word. Compare the 'a' in 'cat' and in 'cake'. Spanish vowels never shift like that. Try saying 'casa' with the same 'a' twice.
Look at 'niño' (child). The mark above the n changes its sound to one you already know from English 'onion'. Say it slowly.
claims: Spanish accent marks show the stressed syllable.

Thinks Spanish has extra vowel sounds like some other languages.

lessons.title: Saying Your Name: Me llamo
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself and ask someone's name, in both formal and informal ways.
lessons.hook: Introducing yourself correctly is the very first thing you will do with your Peruvian team.
lessons.explain: 'Me llamo ___' means 'My name is ___'. Literally it means 'I call myself'. 'Me' means myself, and 'mi' means my. So 'Mi llamo' is incorrect; say 'Me llamo'. To ask a coworker informally, say '¿Cómo te llamas?' To ask formally, say '¿Cómo se llama?' Example: 'Hola, me llamo Alex. ¿Cómo te llamas?'
key_facts: 'Me llamo ___' means 'My name is ___' (literally 'I call myself').
'Me' means myself; 'mi' means my.
'Mi llamo' is incorrect; say 'Me llamo'.
Informal question: '¿Cómo te llamas?'
Formal question: '¿Cómo se llama?'
fixes: Wrote 'Mi llamo Alex' instead of 'Me llamo Alex'.

predict.q: Which do you think means 'My name is Alex'?

angles: Think of 'llamar' as 'to call'. You are calling yourself a name, so the word before 'llamo' must mean 'myself', not 'my'. Which of the two short words is that?
Compare English 'I wash myself' with 'my car'. 'Myself' points back to you; 'my' points to something you own. A name introduction uses the first kind.

misconceptions: Thinks the verb ending doesn't matter.

lessons.title: My and Your: mi, tu, su
lessons.objective: Use mi, tu, su and their plurals with nouns.
lessons.hook: Talking about your job, your team and your office all needs words for 'my' and 'your'.
lessons.explain: 'Mi' means my and 'tu' means your (informal). 'Su' means your (formal, usted) and also his or her. The possessive 'tu' has no accent; 'tú' with an accent means 'you'. For plural nouns, add -s: 'mis' and 'tus'. Example: 'mi trabajo' (my job), 'tu oficina' (your office), 'mis compañeros' (my coworkers), and '¿Es su equipo?' (Is it your team?, said formally).
key_facts: 'mi' = my; 'tu' = your (informal).
'su' = your (formal, usted) and also his/her.
Possessive 'tu' has no accent; 'tú' with an accent means 'you'.
Plurals: 'mis', 'tus'.
angles: Think of 'me' from 'me llamo' as pointing back at yourself, while its look-alike with an 'i' shows ownership, like an English sticker that says 'mine'. Which one goes before 'casa' to say 'my house'?
English 'his' and 'her' are different words, but Spanish uses one word for both, and that same word is used for polite 'your'. Use context to work out who is meant.

items.q: Speaking formally to a client, 'your office' is:
misconceptions: Thinks the accented 'tú' is a possessive.
Thinks the accent makes no difference.
Thinks 'mi' stays the same for plurals.
Thinks only the possessive takes the plural.

items.q: Besides formal 'your', what two meanings can 'su' have?

lessons.title: Ser: Saying What You Are
lessons.objective: Use soy, eres and es to state identity, job and origin.
lessons.hook: 'Who are you, what do you do, where are you from?' are the first questions a new team asks.
lessons.explain: 'Ser' means 'to be' for identity, job and origin. Its forms: 'soy' = I am; 'eres' = you are (informal); 'es' = he/she is, or you are (formal). 'Mi trabajo es...' means 'My job is...'. Note that 'estu' is not a Spanish word. Spanish often drops subject pronouns, so 'Soy ingeniero' means 'I am an engineer'. Example: 'Soy de India. Mi trabajo es interesante.'
key_facts: 'ser' = to be, for identity, job and origin.
'soy' = I am; 'eres' = you are (informal); 'es' = he/she is, you are (formal).
'Mi trabajo es...' = 'My job is...'.
'estu' is not a Spanish word.
Spanish often drops subject pronouns: 'Soy ingeniero' = 'I am an engineer'.

predict.q: Which do you think means 'I am from India'?

angles: Think of the verb as a family. The 'I' member, the 'you' member and the 'he/she' member each have their own short form. Start from 'I' and work out the rest.
In 'Ella es doctora' (She is a doctor), notice which form follows 'ella'. Now replace 'ella' with a thing you own, like 'mi casa'.

lessons.title: Estar: How and Where You Are
lessons.objective: Use estoy, estás and está for feelings and location.
lessons.hook: Answering '¿Cómo estás?' is something you'll do every morning.
lessons.explain: 'Estar' also means 'to be', but it is for feelings, states and location. Its forms: 'estoy' = I am, 'estás' = you are (informal), 'está' = he/she is, or you are (formal). '¿Cómo estás?' asks how you are right now, and you answer 'Estoy bien' (I'm well). For location: 'Estoy en la oficina' means 'I am in the office'.
key_facts: 'estar' = to be, for feelings, states and location.
Forms: 'estoy', 'estás', 'está'.
'¿Cómo estás?' answer: 'Estoy bien.'
Location: 'Estoy en la oficina.'

predict.q: Which do you think answers '¿Cómo estás?'

angles: Ser describes what something is; this verb describes how or where it is right now. Imagine a coworker asks how you feel today. Which verb family does your answer need?
Look at 'Ella está en casa' (She is at home). Swap 'ella' for yourself and change the verb ending to match.

rungs.text: —¿Cómo estás? —Estoy bien. Estoy en la oficina.
Answer '¿Cómo estás?' and say where you are now.

claims: 'Estar' is used for feelings, states and location.

misconceptions: Thinks ser is used for how you feel.
Thinks you repeat the question's form.

items.why: 'está' is used for he/she and formal you.
estar is for feelings, states and location.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Choose ser or estar correctly in common sentences.
lessons.hook: Choosing the wrong 'to be' changes your meaning; it's the most common beginner slip.
lessons.explain: Use ser for what something is: identity, profession, origin. Use estar for how or where something is: feelings, temporary states, location. 'Soy cansado' is wrong; 'Estoy cansado' means 'I am tired'. Location always takes estar, even when it's permanent: 'Lima está en Perú'. Example: 'Soy ingeniera y estoy contenta' means 'I'm an engineer and I'm happy'.
key_facts: ser is for what something is: identity, profession, origin.
estar is for how/where something is: feelings, temporary states, location.
'Soy cansado' is wrong; 'Estoy cansado' = I am tired.
Location always takes estar, even if permanent: 'Lima está en Perú.'

predict.q: Which do you think means 'The office is in Lima'?

angles: Ask yourself: am I saying what this thing is, or how and where it is right now? A label like 'doctor' answers the first question. A mood answers the second.
Mountains never move, yet Spanish still describes where they are with the 'how/where' verb. Apply the same logic to a city on a map.
claims: Location in Spanish uses estar even when it is permanent.

misconceptions: Thinks the I form fits a city.
Thinks the I form of estar fits a city.

items.why: Tiredness is a state, so it takes estar.
estar is for feelings and temporary states.
Tiredness is a state, so it takes estar.

lessons.title: Today, Tomorrow, Yesterday
lessons.objective: Use hoy, mañana and ayer correctly, and tell 'mañana' (tomorrow) apart from 'la mañana' (the morning).
lessons.hook: Mixing up 'today' and 'tomorrow' can make you miss a deadline.
lessons.explain: 'hoy' = today. 'mañana' = tomorrow. 'ayer' = yesterday. With 'la', 'la mañana' means 'the morning', and 'por la mañana' means 'in the morning'. Put them together: 'mañana por la mañana' = tomorrow morning. Example: 'La reunión es hoy, no mañana' means 'The meeting is today, not tomorrow'.
key_facts: 'hoy' = today.
'mañana' = tomorrow.
'ayer' = yesterday.
'la mañana' = the morning; 'por la mañana' = in the morning.
'mañana por la mañana' = tomorrow morning.
angles: Picture three calendar squares: the day before, the current day and the day after. Each has its own Spanish word. The word with ñ is never the middle square.
Some English words change meaning with 'the', like 'present' and 'the present'. One Spanish time word works the same way. Work out what it means with and without 'la'.

'Trabajo por la mañana' means I work:

Thinks the words go in English order.

lessons.title: Work Words and Noun Gender
lessons.objective: Use core workplace nouns with el or la, without slipping English nouns into Spanish sentences.
lessons.hook: Your job, the meeting, the team: these are the words you'll use daily.
lessons.aside: Like Hindi, Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, but a noun's gender often differs between the two languages.
lessons.explain: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine. 'el' means 'the' for masculine nouns, and 'la' means 'the' for feminine nouns. Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine, and nouns ending in -a are usually feminine. Key words: el trabajo = the job/work, la reunión = the meeting, la oficina = the office, el equipo = the team. Don't mix English nouns into Spanish sentences: say 'Mi trabajo', not 'Mi work'. Example: 'El equipo está en la oficina.'
key_facts: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine.
'el' = the (masculine); 'la' = the (feminine).
Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine; -a usually feminine.
el trabajo = the job/work; la reunión = the meeting; la oficina = the office; el equipo = the team.
Don't mix English nouns into Spanish: 'Mi trabajo', not 'Mi work'.
fixes: Wrote 'Mi work' mixing English into Spanish.

predict.q: Which do you guess is correct for 'the house' (casa)?

angles: Look at a noun's last letter for a strong clue. 'Libro' (book) and 'mesa' (table) end differently. Use that clue to choose each one's article.
Imagine a Spanish sentence as a wall built only from Spanish bricks. When an English brick slips in, find the Spanish word that fits in its place.
claims: All Spanish nouns have grammatical gender.

lessons.title: Polite Phrases at Work
lessons.objective: Use usted, please, thanks and repair phrases politely with clients and coworkers.
lessons.hook: Politeness and asking someone to repeat themselves will carry you through your first real calls.
lessons.explain: Usted is the formal 'you', like Hindi 'aap', and tú is the informal 'you', like 'tum'. Use usted with clients and seniors until they switch to tú. 'Por favor' = please, 'gracias' = thank you, 'de nada' = you're welcome. '¿Puede repetir, por favor?' = Can you repeat, please? (formal). 'Disculpe' = excuse me (formal). Example: 'Disculpe, ¿puede repetir, por favor? Gracias.'
key_facts: Usted is formal 'you' (like Hindi 'aap'); tú is informal (like 'tum').
Use usted with clients and seniors until they switch to tú.
'Por favor' = please; 'gracias' = thank you; 'de nada' = you're welcome.
'¿Puede repetir, por favor?' = Can you repeat, please? (formal).
'Disculpe' = excuse me (formal).
angles: Think about how you address an elder relative in Hindi compared with a younger cousin. Spanish makes the same kind of choice. Which form does a new client get?
Picture a fast call where you lose a sentence. You need a polite way to get the speaker's attention, then a request for them to say it again. Build that from this lesson's phrases.
